segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To know, in Spanish, is saber. Saber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Saber. You may have heard in British slang, "he's got savvy", "she's got savvy", have you ever heard that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And that comes from Latin, actually. That slang is coming from Latin. Saber is to know, he's got saber, he's got savvy. Saber is spelled with a B, but in English we are saying savvy, with a V. So we're seeing even that connection between the sounds of V and B crossing between English and Spanish: saber, savvy. So saber is to know. So if you want to say I want to know...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say I don't want to know?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say he wants to know, or she wants to know, or you formal want to know?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You change the -o to -e, and you get quiere. Quiere saber. He doesn't want to know.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Why doesn't he want to know?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to know why he doesn't want to know.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero saber por qué no quiere saber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Quiero saber por qué no quiere saber. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for yes, in Spanish, is sí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is also the word for if. So how do you say if?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I want to know if you want to know. Of course we're speaking formally, this is the one we learned so far. I want to know if you want to know.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero saber si quiere saber. I want to know if he wants to invite me.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the first bit is, I want to know...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Saber, B sound, cause it's a B here.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you see, if you think about it block by block, it's very simple. If we think slowly, we learn very quickly, and the process gets much faster. How do you say imagination?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. I don't want to imagine, I don't want to imagine it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what was to come? And we said that we could remember it if we look at convenient, conveniente, which is like with coming...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to know if she wants to come to the house to visit me. I want to know if she wants to come to the house to visit me. So again, it might be something that looks overwhelming that we can't say, but if we divide it up: I want to know...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good! You put "a" there! Because even though we have "a la casa" there in between, you stayed with the feeling of venir, and you wanted to connect it to the next verb, and you were 100% correct to do that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want to know why she doesn't want to come to the house to visit me. I want to know why she doesn't want to come to the house to visit me. I want to know...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Very good. Well done. Quiero saber por qué no quiere venir a la casa a visitarme. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So what we most want to take away from this is the confidence to try to say what we are almost sure we cannot say, because we have this wonderful advantage as English speakers that we have so much vocabulary that we can convert over to Spanish that we won't realize we can convert over to Spanish until we try it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I will just give you now a couple of sentences for listening practice.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What does it mean if I say: Voy a invitarlo, pero no voy a invitarlo ahora. What did I say? First bit is: Voy a invitarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It could be you, you formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or it, if it can make some sense. I'm going to invite it. Voy a invitarlo. Pero...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But. No voy a invitarlo ahora.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: But I won't invite him now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Quiero iniciarlo ahora. Quiero iniciarlo ahora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And, something missing, though? Quiero iniciarlo ahora.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, I want to start it now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiere iniciarlo ahora. Quiere iniciarlo ahora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Por qué no quiere informarme? ¿Por qué no quiere informarme?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Why doesn't he want to let me know, to inform me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, perfect! But this is perfect, what you did. You found the, you got the meaning and you said it how it's comfortable for you in English. Exactly. Why doesn't he want to inform me? Why doesn't he want to let me know? Perfect.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Justificar. I'm not trying to justify myself. I'm not trying to justify myself. What is myself in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Same as me. Same as me. So, I'm not trying...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No intento justificarme. But, I want to explain. Now, explain is an exception.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have explanation in English, but this in Spanish is explicación. It changes, so it's an exception. We don't say explanación, but explicación. We have this in English as well, we have in English inexplicable. How do you say that in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. We have even in English this root of the C sound with explain. We say explain, but then we say inexplicable. So explanation is explicación in Spanish. So how is to explain?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Explicar. So, but I want to explain...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Do you remember how to say something?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Algo, well done. But I want to explain you something. In English maybe it's more common we would say I want to explain something to you, but in Spanish we can just say but I want to explain you something, and let's say it informally. So what was the word for you, for informal? We can remember it from I love you, yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te. Te quiero. So, but I want to explain you something...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Pero quiero explicarte algo. Let's say it all together: I'm not trying to justify myself, but I want to explain something to you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I'm not trying is the first bit. Now, I want 100% of your mental energy on I'm not trying. All of your attention on I'm not trying, then we look at the next bit, and we forget I'm not trying once we've said it, we don't need to hold it. I'm not trying...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We can forget that bit. But...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No intento justificarme, pero quiero explicarte algo. Very good. Well done.
